reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A chronic facial condition centred on the convexities of the central face (cheeks, nose, chin, forehead), typically in fair-skinned middle-aged adults
Cardinal features are persistent central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, and inflammatory papules and pustules
The absence of comedones is a key point distinguishing rosacea from acne vulgaris
Recognise clinical subtypes: erythematotelangiectatic (flushing and redness), papulopustular, phymatous (skin thickening such as rhinophyma), and ocular
Ocular rosacea (grittiness, dryness, blepharitis, conjunctival injection) is common, frequently underdiagnosed, and can threaten vision if untreated
Trigger avoidance is central: sun exposure, heat, hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, and emotional stress commonly provoke flares

Treatment is tailored to subtype, using topical anti-inflammatory agents, oral tetracycline-class antibacterials for their anti-inflammatory effect in papulopustular disease, and laser or light therapy for telangiectasia and erythema
Daily photoprotection and gentle skin care are important adjuncts for all patients
reference.pathophysiology: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disorder of uncertain cause with several contributing mechanisms. Dysregulation of the innate immune system with abnormal cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide processing promotes inflammation and vascular changes. Neurovascular dysregulation drives flushing and persistent erythema, while an increased density of Demodex mites and altered cutaneous microbiome may stimulate the inflammatory response. Ultraviolet radiation, chronic inflammation, and vascular and lymphatic changes contribute to telangiectasia and, over time, the fibrous and sebaceous overgrowth of phymatous disease. Genetic predisposition and environmental triggers modulate expression.
additionalDifferentials: Flushing from carcinoid syndrome or menopause
Contact or photodermatitis of the face
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on morphology and distribution
Ophthalmological assessment when ocular involvement is suspected
Skin biopsy only in atypical cases to exclude lupus or other diagnoses
Investigation for systemic causes of flushing when the history is atypical
Consideration of Demodex assessment in treatment-resistant papulopustular disease
redFlags: Ocular rosacea with pain, photophobia, or visual disturbance suggesting keratitis
Rapidly progressive facial swelling or induration requiring reassessment
Features suggesting lupus or systemic disease rather than rosacea
Disfiguring phymatous change causing functional or psychological impact
reference.prognosis: Rosacea is a chronic relapsing condition that is controllable but not curable; symptoms often persist for years with fluctuating severity, and phymatous changes, once established, tend to be permanent without procedural treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing rosacea as acne and prescribing inappropriate comedolytic-only regimens
Overlooking ocular rosacea and risking corneal complications
Applying potent topical corticosteroids, which can trigger or worsen a rosacea-like eruption
Neglecting trigger identification and photoprotection, leading to persistent flares
